children: OTTAWA--The unemployment rate in Canada held steady at a two-year low last month despite the economy unexpectedly shedding jobs after a strong recovery for the labor market coming into summer.

Employers in the country cut a net 41,700 jobs in August, though with the participation rate dipping slightly and the labor force contracting, the unemployment rate remained at 6.4%, Statistics Canada said Friday.

The softening of the labor market comes after 180,300 jobs were added between May and July, following a weak start to the year, which helped pull the jobless rate down half a percentage point from the recent 6.9% high in April.
The consensus forecast among economists had been for an unchanged unemployment rate and a modest 15,000 rise in employment.
Job losses in August were largely in full-time positions and concentrated among core-age men. Manufacturing was the only sector to record any significant rise in employment for the month.
When calculated using U.S. Labor Department methodology, Canada's unemployment rate was unchanged for a third straight month at 5.3%.

Wage growth also continued to cool in August, adding to disinflationary signals from the job market. Average hourly wages rose 2% from a year earlier, after climbing 2.8% in July and 3.3% in June. That puts wage growth below the pace of consumer price inflation, which has accelerated to 3%.

Canada's economy exited the second quarter looking much stronger that in recent periods, buoyed in part by resilient household spending and recovery in business investment. The outlook has clouded since after trade talks between Ottawa and Washington broke down and the U.S. administration in late August imposed new tariffs on imports from Canada.

The Bank of Canada doesn't expect the new U.S. levies will have a large direct effect on the broader economy, and support programs introduced by Canada's government will likely mitigate some of the damage. Still, the central bank, already wary of the threat to inflation from elevated fuel prices, has warned added uncertainty could lead businesses to delay investment and hiring decisions.
Canada's labor force shrank by 36,800 in August but was 86,800 larger than a year prior.

The participation rate--the proportion of the working-age population who were either employed or unemployed--edged down to 65% from 65.1%. At the same time, the employment rate, the proportion of the working-age population that is employed, eased to 60.8% from 60.9%.

Among the roughly 1.5 million people without a job last month, 24% were in long-term unemployment, meaning they had been continuously searching for work for 27 weeks or more. That is a similar proportion to a year ago, but remained above the roughly 17% average before the Covid-19 pandemic from 2017 to 2019.
The layoff rate in the country stood at 0.8%, slightly below the 1% recorded a year earlier but similar to the pre-pandemic period.
Full-time employment in Canada fell by 35,900 during August, while part time jobs declined by 5,800.

The number of private-sector employees dropped by 22,800 during the month, while the number of public-sector workers was down by 20,000. The ranks of the self-employed were nudged up by 1,100 last month.
